📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

Sources indicate that the torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

It has been revealed that the Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

Industry observers note that to look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We blueprint to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

According to recent reports, select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:.

No need for torchrun: the script rolls out its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

According to recent reports, A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:.

Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel proposal use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

In a recent development, at the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS indicates nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

Everything the Space highlights comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:.

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

Keep inference running through regional capacity shortfalls with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2121 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that serving a model from more than one AWS Region is a well-established pattern for highly available inference: when one Region runs short of GPU capacity, requests move to another.
  • Recent findings suggest that today, we’re introducing cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI.
  • In this post, we explain how cross-Region inference routing decides where each request runs, walk through an example with one model in two Regions, and cover monitoring, limits, and what you pay.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that serving a model from more than one AWS Region is a well-established pattern for highly available inference: when one Region runs short of GPU capacity, requests move to another. The pattern is simple to describe and hard to operate. Until now, if you served models on Amazon SageMaker AI managed endpoints, cross-Region routing was a piece you still had to build yourself.

Recent findings suggest that today, we’re introducing cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI. It uses a latest resource, the inference router, that gives your application one invocation path across the endpoints and inference components you already run, in one or more AWS Regions and AWS accounts. You register the destinations that serve a model, and your application invokes the router instead of a specific endpoint. The router keeps requests in its own Region while the local destination is healthy, shifts new requests to another registered destination when it isn’t, and returns traffic gradually after recovery.

In this post, we explain how cross-Region inference routing decides where each request runs, walk through an example with one model in two Regions, and cover monitoring, limits, and what you pay. For a cross-account deployment that serves several models, see How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI.

A SageMaker AI endpoint runs in one AWS Region and one account. When autoscaling can’t add instances of the type your endpoint needs, requests throttle and time out, even when the same model has spare capacity in another Region. To use that capacity, your application must detect a struggling endpoint and switch Regions, decide which errors are safe to retry without running the model twice, move traffic back after recovery without flapping, and manage access to endpoints in other accounts. That code sits on the critical path of every request, and every team serving models across Regions maintains its own version of it.

Cross-Region inference routing is based on a few core ideas:.

A few terms describe the pieces:.

The Region you create the router in is its local Region. To prefer a different Region, create a router there. The router doesn’t create capacity, scale your endpoints, deploy models, or copy model artifacts and container images. Each destination must already be running in its Region.

Figure 1: Each request goes to a healthy destination, with the router preferring destinations in its own Region.

The router considers only destinations that are registered on the routing target and that it’s authorized to invoke. Among those, it prefers destinations in its own Region, and when more than one local destination is healthy, it spreads requests across them evenly. Requests leave the Region only when local destinations can’t serve reliably. To detect that, SageMaker AI calculates a health score for each destination from its recent requests, measured in the destination’s own Region. Server errors (5xx), throttles, and timeouts lower the score. Errors from the SageMaker AI platform (for example, failed health check) lower it the most. Errors caused by the request itself, such as invalid input, don’t lower it, because the same request would fail in any Region. Model latency isn’t an input, so an endpoint that keeps returning successful responses keeps its traffic. Signals such as failed instance rolls out or an endpoint running fewer instances than its autoscaling target make the router react faster, but only after the destination starts failing requests.

The router evaluates each destination’s health and publishes it to Amazon CloudWatch as one of three states. A healthy destination serves normally. An overloaded destination still serves, and the router moves part of its traffic away. A degraded destination is failing or can’t serve, so the router moves most of its traffic away and keeps a small share to detect recovery.

Figure 2: How each destination health state changes the traffic the router sends to it.

SageMaker AI manages failover thresholds and timing, so you don’t need to tune any thresholds. If health information for remote destinations goes stale, the router keeps traffic in its own Region, so a gap in monitoring never moves traffic on its own.

The more requests fail, the more traffic moves, so a destination need not fail outright first. Traffic starts to move within about a minute of sustained errors, or longer for a destination with little traffic. Traffic that leaves the local Region is spread across the healthy remote destinations in proportion to their health. You can’t set weights or a fallback order. After recovery, traffic returns over several minutes, more slowly than it left. Requests in progress aren’t interrupted.

Sources indicate that when a destination fails a real-time request without running the model, the router retries that request once on a different destination. This covers, for example, a throttle, a 503 error, a model that isn’t ready, a rejection by a cross-Region traffic cap, or access denied by the destination. The router never retries timeouts, 500 errors, or model errors.

For asynchronous requests, the router tries each eligible destination once, local destinations first, until one accepts the request.

Figure 3: The router retries a real-time request once on another destination, and only when the model didn’t run.

Figure 4 shows where requests were served in one of our tests with a test model.

Figure 4: Where requests were served as the local endpoint was overloaded, a destination in another account lost and regained access, and the local endpoint recovered.

The following use cases show common ways to use cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI.

Sources indicate that when a destination belongs to a different account than the router, both accounts must allow each request. On the endpoint side, the owner attaches a resource-based policy that allows the router account to invoke the endpoint, and the sagemaker:SourceInferenceRouterArn condition key limits that access to one named router. The following policy allows only my-router in account 444455556666 to invoke the endpoint. Its second statement has no router condition and lets the router account read the endpoint’s status. Without that statement, the destination shows its status as unknown.

According to recent reports, in the router account, callers need sagemaker:InvokeInferenceRouter (or sagemaker:InvokeInferenceRouterAsync) on the router and sagemaker:InvokeEndpoint (or sagemaker:InvokeEndpointAsync) on every destination, because the router invokes each destination on the caller’s behalf. A router never gives a caller access to an endpoint they couldn’t call directly. For DescribeInferenceRouter to report each destination’s status, callers also need sagemaker:DescribeEndpoint on endpoints and sagemaker:DescribeInferenceComponent on inference components. Applications in other accounts call the router by assuming a role in the router account. For a walkthrough, see How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI and User Guide on cross-account destinations.

Figure 5: Controls the endpoint owner keeps: an endpoint policy that allows one named router, and an optional cross-Region traffic cap.

It has been revealed that when the router moves requests away from a Region that’s short on capacity, those requests land on endpoints that already serve their own Region’s callers. By default, a receiving endpoint accepts any amount of cross-Region traffic, so a surge of overflow can push it into throttling. With a cross-Region traffic cap, the endpoint owner decides how much of the endpoint’s capacity other Regions might use.

According to recent reports, you set the cap in CreateEndpointConfig with CrossRegionTrafficConfig, which takes two required values. MaxInvocationsPerSecondPerInstance is the number of invocations per second that one instance can take, which you measure with a load test of your model, instance type, and typical payload. MaxCrossRegionPercentPerEndpoint is the share of that capacity that other Regions might use. SageMaker AI multiplies the per-instance rate by the instances in service and applies the percentage, so the cap follows autoscaling. For example, with 50 invocations per second per instance, a 20 percent cap, and 4 instances in service, the endpoint accepts up to 40 requests per second from other Regions. When autoscaling adds 2 instances, the cap rises to 60 requests per second.

It has been revealed that only requests from other Regions count against the cap. Requests from the endpoint’s own Region, including direct InvokeEndpoint calls and calls from a router in the same Region, are never throttled by it. When cross-Region requests exceed the cap, the endpoint rejects the extra requests before your model runs, and the router retries each one once on a different destination. If no other destination can take the request, your application gets a throttling error.

In a recent development, the cap applies to real-time endpoints, and all inference components on an endpoint share it. For an endpoint that hosts inference components, load test one instance with its usual mix of inference components and payloads to measure MaxInvocationsPerSecondPerInstance, and run the test again when that mix or your payloads change. If you leave out CrossRegionTrafficConfig, the endpoint accepts any amount of cross-Region traffic.

It has been revealed that in this example, we deploy Qwen3-4B with the vLLM container as an inference component in US East (Ohio) and US West (Oregon), in one account. Because the inference router doesn’t support response streaming, the application sends non-streaming requests, and each request must complete within about a minute, the same limit as InvokeEndpoint. We then create a router in US East (Ohio) with one routing target that lists both:.

Run DescribeInferenceRouter and confirm that each destination’s RoutingStatus is Routable before you send traffic.

The application invokes the router with the routing target name and the same payload it would send to InvokeEndpoint, and reads the serving destination and routing reason from the response:.

Traffic stayed in US East (Ohio) while its inference component ran, moved to US West (Oregon) with no change to the application when we removed it, and came back after we restored it.

The complete notebook for this example is available on GitHub.

Tip: Use instance pools and cross-Region inference routing together. With a capacity-aware instance pool, SageMaker AI can use another instance type in the same Region at creation and during scale-out. The router moves fresh requests to another Region when the local endpoint as a whole can’t serve. For details, see Capacity-aware inference: Automatic instance fallback for SageMaker AI endpoints.

The inference router gives you two views of routing: a record on every real-time response and metrics in CloudWatch.

Every real-time response includes the ARN of the destination that served the request in InvokedRoutedResourceArn, and the routing reason in RoutingReason. The routing reason is one of the following:.

We recommend logging both values with your application’s own request logs.

It has been revealed that asynchronous responses don’t include the serving destination. Router metrics in CloudWatch show where asynchronous requests were placed.

The router publishes OpenTelemetry metrics to CloudWatch in its own account and Region, labeled with the router, routing target, and destination:.

Recent findings suggest that alarm on destinations that aren’t healthy and on the error rate across all error types. See Monitor an inference routers with Amazon CloudWatch and AWS CloudTrail.

Figure 6: Requests per destination from the router’s CloudWatch invocations metric during the test shown in Figure 4.

Each destination endpoint keeps publishing its existing SageMaker AI metrics in its own account and Region. To view them in one place, use CloudWatch cross-account observability and cross-account cross-Region dashboards.

In a recent development, AWS CloudTrail records the router’s API calls (create, update, delete, describe, and list) as management events and router invocations as data events. You enable data events on your trail as you do for other SageMaker AI data events.

Keep the following in mind when you design with the inference router:.

Also note the following limitations:.

Cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI gives your application one invocation path across the endpoints and inference components you already run, in multiple AWS Regions and AWS accounts. The router prefers its own Region, shifts upcoming requests when a destination can’t serve reliably, returns traffic gradually after recovery, and shows you where each request ran and why. Your endpoints, models, containers, and autoscaling policies don’t change.

Cross-Region inference routing is generally available starting today in most commercial AWS Regions (except me-south-1 and me-central-1), for real-time and asynchronous inference.

There is no additional charge for cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI. You pay for the SageMaker AI endpoints and inference components that serve your requests at standard SageMaker AI pricing, whether a request reaches them directly or through an inference router. The inference router publishes metrics to Amazon CloudWatch in the router’s account, and you pay standard CloudWatch rates for those metrics and any queries you run on them. For details, see Amazon SageMaker AI pricing.

To get started, see the Amazon SageMaker AI documentation on cross-Region inference routing and explore the sample notebook on GitHub.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that LFM3 is our upcoming generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence.
  • LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.
  • It has been revealed that LFM2 highlighted that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that LFM3 is our upcoming generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.

It has been revealed that LFM2 highlighted that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:.

Industry observers note that the payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

Sources indicate that every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two newly introduced in-house encoders:.

It has been revealed that each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

Industry observers note that reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:.

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

Sources indicate that reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:.

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Industry observers note that reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a upcoming in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:.

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:.

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:.

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

According to recent reports, reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:.

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:.

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

Recent findings suggest that reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:.

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:.

Recent findings suggest that for brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

Recent findings suggest that we adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video.

Tech Report: Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2054 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, language models can do a lot.
  • Say a customer calls your support line.
  • In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they stated (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Today we're announcing two packages:.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Recent findings suggest that computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

It has been revealed that it's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:.

Sources indicate that the package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:.

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

In a recent development, parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:.

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

Sources indicate that to add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:.

In a recent development, each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Sources indicate that downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

Sources indicate that when you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:.

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:.

Sources indicate that parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

Recent findings suggest that these numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

According to recent reports, anyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't upcoming, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

What's latest is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Industry observers note that apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:.

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

Industry observers note that if you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

According to recent reports, emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:.

The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Sources indicate that reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:.

In a recent development, you use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Recent findings suggest that raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

According to recent reports, each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

AnyDecisionModel has six backends:.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Recent findings suggest that like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

Add the packages to your Package.swift:.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

According to recent reports, try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, cisco, like many large engineering organizations, is adopting generative and agentic AI to change how its engineers build software. The hard part is no longer access to the technology. It’s helping thousands of engineers move from watching a demo to confidently building with it. Recorded sessions and slide decks rarely close that gap. Engineers learn fastest when they build something real, see it fail, fix it, and try again.

AWS designed AWS AI League for exactly that. It turns hands-on AI learning into a gamified competition, where participants customize models and build agents on AWS, get instant feedback on a live leaderboard, and compete in a game-show-style finale.

Recent findings suggest that cisco is one of the clearest examples of what this looks like at scale. In 2025, Hemanth V, a Cisco software engineer, went from an internal Cisco event to being crowned the first AWS AI League Champion at AWS re:Invent 2025. In 2026, 1,200 Cisco engineers competed in an AWS AI League tournament at Cisco Transformation Fest 4.0. The winner, Nishanth Aluhonnu, earned a full event pass to AWS re:Invent 2026 in Las Vegas.

In this post, we share how Cisco and AWS used Cisco Transformation Fest and AWS AI League to build a lasting culture of learning by doing. We previously covered this program in From theory to delivery: How Atos upskilled 400 engineers in agentic AI, and here we look at Cisco’s experience. We walk through Cisco’s journey, share technical lessons from the 2026 winning agent, and explain how your organization can host its own AWS AI League.

AWS AI League helps organizations build advanced AI skills through competition. Each league follows three steps:.

Although AWS AI League offers multiple use cases, at Cisco it offered the following two challenges:.

Finalists are scored on time efficiency, accuracy, agent planning, and token consumption efficiency.

Figure 1: AWS AI League champion at AWS re:Invent 2025.

Figure 2: 2026 AWS AI League winner at Cisco campus.

Recent findings suggest that the AWS AI League story at Cisco grows out of a deep engineering partnership. Cisco and AWS bring together networking, cloud, security, and observability for shared customers including:.

In a recent development, the two companies have also published joint deployment guides and Cisco Validated Designs across networking and AWS. A recent example of co-innovation is SD-WAN fabric on demand across the AWS backbone, built to deliver the resilience and uptime customers expect.

“When you see that many business units independently choosing to build their next-generation platforms natively on AWS, that’s not a vendor relationship anymore. It’s a true engineering partnership.”.

— Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco.

Cisco’s VP of Engineering Kumaril Kapoor and AWS Industries India leader Chandra Balani sit down to discuss the AWS and Cisco partnership story, from co-innovation across networking, cloud, and AI to enabling thousands of engineers through the annual Cisco AWS Transformation Fest.

As the partnership grew, it extended beyond technology to people. Working closely with Cisco teams in India, AWS saw a strong appetite for learning and experimenting among Cisco engineers across many business units. The question was how to scale that impact beyond the day-to-day touchpoints of the partnership.

The answer was Cisco Transformation Fest, first held in 2022. The program is built on five tenets the team summarized as SCALE:.

Figure 3: 2026 Cisco AWS Transformation Fest 4.0 AWS AI League finalists.

Industry observers note that transformation Fest brings together several formats: AWS GameDays, AWS AI League, sessions where Cisco leaders share best practices and success stories with peers, and sessions on Amazon and AWS culture. What began as a single event is now an annual, three-day program that has completed its fourth edition and reached around 2,000 engineers. AWS continues to engage Cisco teams with hands-on workshops and experience-based accelerations.

Sources indicate that “It has been genuinely valuable for us, and it’s really a journey, but I appreciate most is the intent behind it. It’s built around our people. It gives our engineers the time, the space, and the hands-on support to grow real skills on AWS. For us, it has turned into a lasting culture of learning by doing. It’s not a one-off event.”.

— Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco.

Industry observers note that of all the Transformation Fest formats, AWS AI League has had the most visible impact. Its gamified, hands-on structure puts engineers to work with Amazon SageMaker on fine-tuning, model customization and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for agent building, against a clock and in front of their peers. Participants leave with practical experience and genuine confidence in their AI skills.

“This is where enablement actually turns into real execution.”.

— Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco.

Hemanth V, a software engineer in Cisco’s switching core platform team, had an inspiring journey that set the benchmark for Cisco.

Hemanth finished ahead of Ross Williams from Aqfer (second place) and Deepesh Khanna from Capital One (third place).

It has been revealed that “You don’t need to know everything beforehand. You will learn a lot of things on the way. The only thing that matters is your curiosity and willingness to learn.”.

— Hemanth V, Software Engineer, Cisco, and 2025 AWS AI League Champion.

In 2026, Cisco Transformation Fest 4.0 hosted a full AWS AI League agentic AI tournament. The AWS account team ran pre-event training so that engineers with no prior agentic AI experience could compete from day one. The format was designed to narrow a large field down to a single winner:.

Nishanth Aluhonnu, a software engineer at Cisco, finished first at every stage and earned a full conference pass to AWS re:Invent 2026.

The finale itself revealed why the format works. Participants could not change code, tools, or prompts during the finale, only a short steering instruction before each round. Success depended on how well each agent made decisions on maps it had never seen before. Nishanth lost the first round, then won the second by a wide margin by ignoring a board full of low-value coins in favor of a single high-value challenge.

Figure 4: Cisco AWS Transformation Fest 4.0 AWS AI League finalists on stage.

According to recent reports, the 2026 winning agent offers lessons that go well beyond the game. Each design choice maps to a decision teams face when they run agents in production.

The agentic AI challenge scores agents on challenge points, a treasure bonus, remaining lives, and a token bonus, computed as tokenBonus = 1000 - (totalOutputTokens / challengesVisited).

According to recent reports, in the qualifier, the top four agents all solved the map. The first-place agent emitted 1,220 output tokens and the second-place agent emitted 1,430, and the final margin was only 16 points out of nearly 16,000. After every agent can solve the problem, efficiency decides the winner.

In a recent development, to understand which tokens mattered, Nishanth built nine variants of the same agent, changing one thing at a time. The result was clear: tool results and the system prompt didn’t count against the score, but everything the agent wrote, including tool call arguments, did. Each tool call carried roughly 52 tokens of fixed overhead on top of its arguments.

It has been revealed that this mirrors real-world cost. Generating output is sequential and is typically priced several times higher than input, and in an agent loop that cost compounds across every step. A long, well-structured system prompt (which you can also cache) is cheap. A chatty agent isn’t.

Industry observers note that A common architecture for this challenge is a supervisor agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that delegates to specialist sub-agents for navigation, computation, and web retrieval. It’s a sound pattern for many production systems. The winning design used a single agent with no sub-agents. Instead, the prompt began with a short dispatch table that matched each challenge type to the right approach in a single turn.

Sources indicate that the reasoning was simple: every handoff between agents is a message the model has to write, and in this challenge every written token is scored. The lesson isn’t that sub-agents are bad. It’s to choose your architecture based on what coordination costs you. When coordination is expensive, a flatter design can win.

The following diagram shows the AWS reference architecture for the agentic AI challenge: a supervisor agent with specialist sub-agents. The winning design deliberately didn’t use this multi-agent pattern.

Figure 5: AWS AI League reference architecture.

In this reference architecture, a supervisor agent runs in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and coordinates three sub-agents, with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and AgentCore memory connected to the runtime. The supervisor and sub-agents route through the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to four tools: a navigation tool, browser tool, code execution tool, and custom tools using AWS Lambda functions.

Route planning was not left to the model. It ran in an AWS Lambda function that treated the board as an optimization problem. Each tile carried an expected value: the points it paid, minus the lives it could cost, minus the tokens the agent would spend to solve it. The planner respected constraints, such as collecting a key before its door, and refined the route within a time budget.

This is a useful pattern for most agents: let the model handle language and judgment, and move search, math, and rules into tools where they are faster, cheaper, and repeatable.

The second finale round was designed as a trap. A seven-by-seven board was almost entirely covered in coins worth 25 points each, while a single scheduling challenge tile was worth 1,500 points. Habit noted to collect the coins. The planner’s value table said the coins were noise. The agent went for the high-value challenge and scored 7,537 points in that round, compared with 5,953 for the next finalist. That round built the lead that carried the agent to the overall win.

Across two years of AWS AI League at Cisco, the impact shows up in skills, culture, and recognition:.

For Hemanth, the biggest takeaway was confidence. You do not need to master everything before you start. You learn by getting hands-on.

Industry observers note that “Technology alone isn’t enough. You need people who are empowered to experiment with it. Transformation Fest created that enablement environment, and AWS AI League created the opportunity for execution.”.

— Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco.

According to recent reports, in this post, we showed how Cisco and AWS turned enablement into execution. Cisco Transformation Fest created a space for engineers to learn by doing, and AWS AI League gave them a real challenge, a scoreboard, and a stage. The result is a culture of hands-on AI building that reaches thousands of engineers.

We look forward to seeing what your teams build.

Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1590 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral.
  • There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team.
  • Recent findings suggest that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:.

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Recent findings suggest that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Recent findings suggest that mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That noted, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

According to recent reports, for community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

According to recent reports, mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

Industry observers note that for each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

It has been revealed that cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:.

Recent findings suggest that mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing demonstrated promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

The 2-bit quants run on a single Apple Silicon Ultra computer with 512 GB of unified RAM. The others require distributed inference. You can also run on multiple NVIDIA or AMD cards.

Industry observers note that mistral Large 4 is also available on Inference Endpoints, with a ready-to-deploy recipe on 8 x NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The recipe runs vLLM with the FP8 weights split across all eight GPUs using tensor and expert parallelism, and uses the model's built-in DSpark draft head for faster generation through speculative decoding. #7546. Optimize AI economics on Amazon Bedrock with Accenture’s sequenced approach

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1973 w)

Optimize AI economics on Amazon Bedrock with Accenture’s sequenced approach

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1973 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As enterprises scale AI on Amazon Bedrock, token spend often grows even as per-token prices fall.
  • In this post, you will learn about six levers for optimizing token spend, how Accenture applied them in production, and how to apply them using Amazon Bedrock.
  • In a recent development, accenture applied these levers in four client engagements across telecom, insurance, mining, and a large enterprise deployment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As enterprises scale AI on Amazon Bedrock, token spend often grows even as per-token prices fall. Without cost allocation tags in place, your cloud invoice shows AI spend as a single line item rather than by team, workload, agent, or model. Cheaper tokens expand adoption, and agentic workloads multiply invocations. As successful AI use cases scale, consumption can rise faster than unit prices drop. The economic question is whether the business value generated grows faster than the cost of the intelligence required to produce it. The Linux Foundation has launched the Tokenomics Foundation to develop open standards for AI cost economics, a sign that managing the economics of AI is now an industry discipline.

In this post, you will learn about six levers for optimizing token spend, how Accenture applied them in production, and how to apply them using Amazon Bedrock.

In a recent development, accenture applied these levers in four client engagements across telecom, insurance, mining, and a large enterprise deployment. The same levers are available natively on Amazon Bedrock as described in this post. Where savings were measured, token spend fell by about 40–85 percent. Results are specific to each client’s workload and may vary. Client names are withheld by Accenture to protect client confidentiality.

Sources indicate that before you optimize anything, you need to see where consumption is occurring, who owns it, and what business value it produces. Cost allocation tags at the team, workload, and agent level are the prerequisite for connecting consumption to accountable owners and, ultimately, to business outcomes. You apply them through Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles, one profile per application or workload, tagged by team, cost center, and environment. After you activate them as cost allocation tags in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console, you can use these tags to trace which teams, applications, and agents are driving spend. They also make it possible to measure the impact of each change you introduce.

According to recent reports, three AWS services provide the underlying telemetry. AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR 2.0), delivered through AWS Data Exports, handle financial attribution, breaking down billed inference cost by workload and team after your cost allocation tags are active. Amazon CloudWatch captures operational signals such as invocation counts and latency. Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging records request-level detail, including the model used and the input and output token counts for each call.

Telemetry alone isn’t enough. Engineers can read cost per invocation on a dashboard, but product owners and program leaders need a metric expressed in business terms. Accenture’s Cost per Business Transaction (CpBT) framework bridges this gap. CpBT aggregates all the model invocations, retries, tool calls, and agent handoffs that contribute to one successful business output into a single fully loaded cost figure. It surfaces the true cost of producing a result, including the failed attempts that raw token pricing hides. Tracked against the business value each workflow delivers, CpBT distinguishes a growing bill that reflects scaling success from one that reflects waste.

Industry observers note that the goal of these six levers isn’t to minimize tokens at all costs. It’s to use the right amount and level of intelligence to deliver each business outcome at the appropriate cost, quality, and risk. The levers are organized into three phases based on the complexity of the change and the investment it requires. AWS and Accenture recommend working through the phases in order, and you can apply each phase independently to the workloads where it will have the most impact.

According to recent reports, with Amazon Bedrock prompt caching, the model reuses the parts of a prompt that repeat across requests, such as system instructions, tool definitions, and reference documents, so you stop paying full price to process the same content again. Amazon Bedrock stores the key-value state of previously computed prompt prefixes and is designed to skip recomputation on later requests. This is designed to reduce cached input token costs by up to 90 percent for supported models (see Amazon Bedrock Prompt Caching).

It has been revealed that amazon Bedrock batch inference processes non-urgent workloads asynchronously as a group at 50 percent lower cost than on-demand pricing for select models (see Amazon Bedrock Pricing). You submit inference requests as a batch job, and results are written to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) when processing completes. Batch inference suits nightly reports, document processing pipelines, and evaluation runs that don’t need an immediate response.

Both levers add configuration to your existing setup. Prompt caching requires cache checkpoint markers in your prompts, and batch inference requires submitting eligible requests as a batch job instead of calling the on-demand API. Apply caching to interactive, on-demand traffic and batch inference to asynchronous work. Neither requires new infrastructure or architecture changes.

Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing directs requests across models within the same family, matching each task to the level of intelligence its business value, complexity, and risk require, rather than defaulting every request to the most powerful model. Intelligent prompt routing can reduce costs by up to 30 percent without compromising accuracy (see Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing). Check Amazon Bedrock Pricing for any routing charges. In the following engagements, Accenture’s model tiering and triage routing apply this same routing lever.

Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) optimization tunes the retrieval step in the RAG process so that fewer unnecessary context tokens reach the model. Techniques such as hierarchical chunking, metadata-based filtering, and reranking narrow the retrieved context to the most relevant chunks, so you pay primarily for content that improves the answer.

Two complementary Accenture patterns work alongside these AWS native levers. Context scoping limits the data each agent receives to the document slice relevant to its step of the workflow, rather than passing the full case context at every handoff. Context compression summarizes or filters documents before they reach the model. Both reduce input token volume, especially across multi-agent chains.

In a recent development, semantic caching stores responses and reuses them when a newly introduced request is semantically similar to one already answered, even if the wording differs. This avoids redundant model invocations and reduces both cost and latency. On AWS, you can implement it with a vector store such as Amazon ElastiCache in front of the model. In an AWS benchmark on 63,796 real chatbot queries, a 0.90 similarity threshold produced a 74.5 percent cache hit rate, 92.3 percent accuracy, and 72.5 percent cost savings (see ElastiCache semantic caching benchmarks). As you apply routing and semantic caching, keep Amazon Bedrock Guardrails on every route, and set semantic cache expiry so that users don’t receive outdated answers.

Model distillation transfers knowledge from a large teacher model to a smaller, faster student model. Distilled models in Amazon Bedrock are up to 500 percent faster and up to 75 percent less expensive than original models, with less than 2 percent accuracy loss for use cases such as RAG. Distillation is best suited to stable, high-volume workloads where the transaction volume justifies the training investment.

Accenture applied these levers in four client engagements. Each engagement targeted a different cost pattern. In two of them, Accenture applied several changes together, so those results reflect the combined effect rather than any single lever.

Sources indicate that the first engagement was a large enterprise deployment where every request went to a frontier model, with no caching, model tiering, or batching. Accenture applied three changes together: model tiering to match each task to the smallest model that could handle it well, prompt caching for repeated context, and batch processing for overnight and non-urgent jobs. Together they cut monthly token cost by 85 percent, and the saving was not separated by change. About 15 percent of tasks still needed the top model for hard, open-ended reasoning, and the rest ran on lighter models. Your split will depend on your workload composition.

In a recent development, the second engagement was a telecom operator with $12 million in annual token spend. Most of that spend came from agents fanning out requests without limits and from every request going to a frontier model regardless of complexity. Accenture applied triage routing, semantic caching, and context compression together. Input tokens fell by 70 percent, and annual token spend fell from $12 million to $3.8 million, a 68 percent reduction. Accenture validated output quality against the operator’s pre-change performance benchmarks.

In a recent development, the third and fourth engagements each applied a single cache layer. An insurer used model-layer prefix caching, reusing the static portions of its prompts across invocations. A mining operator used an application-layer semantic cache, returning stored responses for repeated queries before they reached the model. Across the two engagements, token spend fell by about 40 percent combined, without model routing changes or training investment.

Sources indicate that outcomes ranged from about 40 percent to about 85 percent, reflecting each client’s starting point. The large enterprise deployment began with no optimization in place and reached 85 percent. The telecom operator reached 68 percent on $12 million in annual token spend, and the insurer and mining operator reached about 40 percent combined with one caching lever each. Results are specific to each client’s workload and may vary.

These savings aren’t the end goal. They create capacity to scale AI workloads, reinvest in higher-value use cases, and improve the return generated by each dollar of AI consumption. Two of these engagements applied several changes at once. When you apply one lever at a time, you can attribute each result to a specific change. AWS and Accenture recommend this sequence for your own workloads: connect consumption to owners and outcomes, apply one lever at a time, measure cost, quality, and business value, and build on what works.

Optimizing AI economics in production requires an ongoing governance cycle spanning cost, quality, risk, and business value, not a one-time technical change. Before you apply any lever, establish a quantitative baseline for both cost and quality so that you can measure the impact of each change against a known starting point. When you validate output quality, use held-out evaluation sets drawn from your actual production traffic rather than synthetic benchmarks. Apply one lever at a time per workload so that you can attribute results to a specific change and roll back cleanly if quality drops below your acceptable thresholds. If you operate in a regulated industry such as financial services, insurance, or healthcare, document your quality test results and rollback procedures as part of your standard change management record.

These four tenets apply regardless of which levers you are using or what phase of the sequencing you are in. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is an environment where you can build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. It includes AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that provides batch evaluation to support your quality validation cycle as you progress through more advanced levers.

You can begin with three steps. First, turn on cost attribution for Amazon Bedrock by applying cost allocation tags at the team and workload level so that your spend is traceable from day one. Second, activate those tags in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console. Then use CUR 2.0 and model invocation logging to identify high-consumption workloads, and assess each one based on spend, business value, quality requirements, risk, volume, and optimization potential. Third, apply Amazon Bedrock prompt caching to that workload’s interactive traffic and Amazon Bedrock batch inference to its asynchronous jobs as configuration-only changes, and measure the result before you move to architectural changes in Phase 2.

In a recent development, the AWS Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens includes model invocation and token cost optimization (AGENTCOST02), a focus area within the cost optimization pillar for agentic workloads. This focus area provides a structured framework you can use to apply these levers at scale across your organization.
